g10-geography-ug7-t1.overview: Africa is the fastest urbanizing continent in the world, yet much of its urban growth is unplanned and unregulated. This lesson explains what urbanization is, why African cities grow without effective planning, and the slums, infrastructure gaps, economic, health and social consequences that follow.
objectives: Define urbanization and explain how it changes both the urban area and the population living there
Name Africa's megacities and describe the continent's pace and pattern of urban growth
Explain the causes of unplanned urbanization in Africa
Analyze the slum, infrastructure, economic, health and social consequences of unplanned urbanization
Apply the concepts of unplanned urbanization to the case of Addis Ababa and other Ethiopian cities
g10-geography-ug7-t1.simple: Urbanization is the shift of population from rural to urban areas, together with the growth of towns and cities. Growth is good only when managed: cities should offer electricity, roads, drinking water, communication, health and education services before population floods in. Africa is still largely rural but is urbanizing fastest of all continents, and much of its expansion is unplanned. Causes include unplanned growth, the legacy of colonialism, international policy pressure and weak planning institutions. The results are slums and squatter settlements, poor infrastructure, high living costs with about 60 percent informal jobs, health risks and social instability. The Addis Ababa case study shows how settlements that emerge without a master plan block proper city development.
g10-geography-ug7-t1.detailed:
What urbanization is. Urbanization refers to the population shift from rural to urban areas and the corresponding decrease in the proportion of people living in rural areas. It does not only denote the growth of the area of towns but also the growth of the population living there. For urbanization to succeed, big cities and small towns alike must have basic physical facilities such as electricity, roads, drinking water, communication, health and education services. Such infrastructure appears when effective management comes before rapid urbanization, and Africa is facing exactly this management problem.

Growth, benefits and risks. As cities grow in population size, spatial extent and density, their environmental and ecological footprints increase. Urban expansion into forests, wetlands and agricultural systems causes habitat clearing, degradation and fragmentation, while consumptive urban lifestyles raise air, water and soil pollution; unplanned urbanization is therefore a root cause of damage to the environment and nature. Yet urbanization is by no means bad in itself: well managed cities are efficient and effective, allow economies of scale, and their proximity and diversity of people spark innovation and create employment. The main factor driving rapid urbanization is rural-urban migration, driven by the prospect of greater employment opportunities and the hope of a better life. When planning cannot cope with the influx, the result in extreme cases is widespread poverty, while unplanned expansion creates big slums, socio-economic disparities and poor sanitary conditions that help diseases spread.

Africa's urban picture. Though Africa is still largely rural, it is one of the fastest urbanizing continents. Its urban population is expected to reach 2.5 billion in 2050, about 21 percent of the world's projected urban population. The continent currently has seven megacities with over 10 million people each: Cairo, Kinshasa, Lagos, Accra, Johannesburg-Pretoria, Khartoum and Nairobi. Many African countries also show a high degree of urban primacy, meaning one city, usually the capital, holds population, economic activity and political power several times greater than the next largest city.

Causes of unplanned urbanization. Unplanned urbanization in Africa results from unplanned and unregulated growth, the legacy of colonialism, the policy pressure of international institutions such as the structural adjustment program of the IMF, the pressure of developed countries through neoliberal policies toward developing countries, and weak urban planning institutions. These underlying processes differ vastly from those in other rapidly urbanizing regions of the world.

Slums, squatters and poor infrastructure. Random, unexpected growth spreads unlawful residential settlements, made worse by fast-paced industrialization, lack of developed land for housing, a large influx of rural immigrants seeking a better life, and land prices far beyond what the urban poor can pay. Infrastructure then fails to keep pace with population growth: transportation infrastructure is very weak, electric power supply and distribution are inadequate, water supply and sewage are in serious shortage, and communications infrastructure is weak, while tight national budgets limit investment.

Economic, health and social consequences. Urban residents face very high costs of housing, food and transportation, together with high unemployment; about 60 percent of urban jobs are in the informal or grey economy, which is neither taxed nor monitored by the government. Urbanization also exacerbates health risks such as obesity and respiratory diseases, and many urban dwellers lack adequate sanitation; high density, poverty and missing infrastructure foster conditions for communicable diseases at a speed that challenges the health sector. Rapid and unplanned growth further leads to urban violence and social unrest, driven by widening inequality, competition for scarce resources such as land, violation of law and weak city governance, while high density fuels house prices and shortages of affordable housing feed the disregard of the urban poor and more crime.

Climate change and the Addis Ababa case. Rapid, inadequate and poorly planned expansion leaves African urban populations highly exposed to climate change; extreme weather partly drives rural-urban migration, and cities near the sea or natural waterways face greater flooding risk, so resilience must be a priority for local governments and the private sector. In Ethiopia, which has experienced the fastest rates of urbanization, Addis Ababa grew from villages that evolved into a major urban settlement without a master plan, with informal settlement at the very heart of its genesis. Two unplanned settlement types exist there: slums in highly congested areas with deteriorated infrastructure, an unsanitary environment and substandard materials, where more than two-thirds of the city's population is believed to live; and squatter settlements built illegally on open space, farmland, steep slopes, along river buffers and roadsides without legal title deed, especially on the urban periphery. Their proliferation prevents planned development and promotes spontaneous horizontal expansion of the city.

keyTerms.def: The population shift from rural to urban areas, involving the growth of the urban area and of the population living there.
Urban growth that occurs randomly and without regulation, leading to environmental degradation, slums, poverty and poor services.
A situation in which one city, usually the capital, holds population, economic activity and political power several times greater than the next largest city.
A city with a population over 10 million; Africa's seven are Cairo, Kinshasa, Lagos, Accra, Johannesburg-Pretoria, Khartoum and Nairobi.
A highly congested unplanned settlement with deteriorated infrastructure, unsanitary environment and housing of substandard materials, mostly inhabited by low-income groups.
A settlement built illegally, without legal title deed, on open space, farmland, steep slopes, river buffers or roadsides, mainly on the urban periphery.
The lasting inherited weakness of urban institutions and structures left by colonial rule, cited as a cause of unplanned African urban growth.
The advantages that can occur as a result of increasing the size of a business, one of the benefits of well managed cities.

workedExamples.problem: Africa's urban population is projected to reach 2.5 billion in 2050, which will be 21 percent of the world's projected urban population. Estimate the world's projected urban population for 2050.
workedExamples.given: Africa's projected urban population = 2.5 billion; Africa's share of the world's projected urban population = 21% = 0.21.
workedExamples.formula: World projected urban population = Africa's projected urban population / Africa's share.
workedExamples.answer: About 11.9 billion people; Africa alone would then hold roughly one-fifth of the world's urban dwellers.

workedExamples.problem: A town with 200,000 residents grows to 260,000 in ten years while its water supply and roads were planned for the old size. Compute the growth rate and state the likely consequences.
workedExamples.given: Old population = 200,000; new population = 260,000; infrastructure unchanged.
workedExamples.formula: Growth rate = (new population - old population) / old population x 100.
workedExamples.calculation: 0.30 x 100 = 30 percent unplanned growth in ten years.
workedExamples.answer: 30 percent growth without planning; expect insufficient water availability, waste-disposal problems, urban sprawl and declining air and water quality.

workedExamples.problem: In Addis Ababa, family A occupies farmland on the urban periphery without a legal title deed, while family B lives in a congested inner-city neighbourhood of substandard houses with broken sanitation. Identify each settlement type.
workedExamples.given: Family A: illegal occupation, periphery, no title deed. Family B: congested centre, deteriorated infrastructure, substandard materials.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: illegal peripheral building without title deed is a squatter settlement; congested central housing with deteriorated infrastructure is a slum.
workedExamples.substitution: Family A's home is built unlawfully on farmland at the edge; family B's home is in a crowded, deteriorated central area.
workedExamples.calculation: Matching each description to its definition separates the two types cleanly.
workedExamples.answer: A is a squatter settlement; B is a slum.

commonMistakes: Defining urbanization only as the growth of town area, forgetting that the population living there must also grow.
Concluding that urbanization is always bad, when well managed cities bring economies of scale, innovation and jobs.
Using the words slum and squatter settlement interchangeably; slums are congested central areas while squatter settlements are built illegally on the periphery without title deeds.
Blaming only rural-urban migration for unplanned growth while ignoring the colonial legacy, the IMF structural adjustment program and neoliberal policy pressure.
Thinking urban primacy means a country has two similarly large cities; it means one dominant city outweighs the next largest several times.
Assuming infrastructure automatically expands as fast as the population; in Africa transport, power, water, sewage and communications all lag behind.
Forgetting that cities near the sea or natural waterways face extra flooding risk under climate change.
applications: Explaining why spontaneously emerging squatter settlements in Addis Ababa appear on steep slopes, river buffers and roadsides at the city's edge.
Checking whether new Ethiopian town plans provide electricity, roads, water, communication, health and education services before rapid growth arrives.
Analyzing how rising house prices in Addis Ababa push low-income families into overcrowded or informal housing and raise urban crime.
Arguing for slum upgrading and municipal services, since more than two-thirds of Addis Ababa's residents are believed to live in slums.
Assessing flood risk for Ethiopian cities located along rivers and for African coastal cities exposed to extreme weather.
Comparing Addis Ababa's spontaneous horizontal expansion with the benefits a master plan would offer for land use and services.
g10-geography-ug7-t1.summary: Urbanization means the shift of people to urban areas and the growth of both urban space and urban population, and it benefits society only when planning and infrastructure come first. Africa, still largely rural, is urbanizing fastest and by 2050 will hold 2.5 billion urban residents and seven megacities, but unplanned growth rooted in the colonial legacy and weak institutions produces slums, squatter settlements, infrastructure gaps, informal economies, disease and social instability. The Addis Ababa case shows how settlements built without a master plan block orderly city development.

g10-geography-ug7-t2.overview: Migration is the movement of people who leave one place to establish a new residence somewhere else. This lesson defines the forms of migration, separates the push factors that lie at African origins from the pull factors at destinations, and traces how migration, including slave trade migrations, has shaped Africa's population.
objectives: Define human migration and distinguish internal from international migration
Distinguish voluntary from forced migration using African examples
Analyze the economic, political and social push factors at African origins
Analyze the pull factors that attract migrants to their destinations
Evaluate the impacts of migration, including the slave trade, on Africa's demographic landscape
g10-geography-ug7-t2.simple: Migration is the permanent change of residence by an individual or a group, and it may cross a district line or an international boundary. Internal migration, such as moving from a rural area to a city, is distinct from international migration between countries. Migration can also be voluntary, undertaken to seek better economic opportunities or a good life, or forced, when people are expelled by war, drought, famine, natural disasters or political conflict. Push factors drive people away from their origin: poverty, low wages, unemployment, poor governance, corruption, instability and civil strife. Pull factors beckon at the destination: better income, security, education and health care. Historical slave trade migrations between the 16th and 19th centuries greatly reduced Africa's population.
g10-geography-ug7-t2.detailed:
What migration is. Human migration is the permanent change of residence by an individual or a group of people, and it can occur within a country or across an international boundary. Migration is an essential component of population change and structure, unlike natural increase, which depends on birth rates and mortality. People migrate to establish a permanent or semi-permanent residence at a destination, and their motives range from the pure desire to experience life in another place to the obligation to move to avoid risks found in the area of origin.

Forms of migration. Migration falls into several broad categories. First, internal and international migration are distinguished: movements of individuals and families from one area of a country to another, for example from rural areas to the cities, differ from movements from one country to another. Second, migration may be voluntary or forced. Most voluntary migration, whether internal or external, is undertaken in search of better economic opportunities or the good life, while forced migrations usually involve people expelled by war, drought, famine, natural disasters or other political conflicts.

Push factors at the origin. The causes of migration are a complex web of factors expressed as push and pull. In Africa, multiple push factors spur migration both within the continent and to other regions. Economic push factors include poor socio-economic conditions, low wages, high levels of unemployment and poverty, and these are usually brought about by a mismatch between rapid population growth and the available resources, together with a low level of requisite technology and capacity to create employment at the origin. Political and social factors create further fertile ground: poor governance, corruption, political instability, conflict and civil strife are major causes of migration for both skilled and unskilled workers.

Pull factors at the destination. The real or perceived opportunity for a better life, high income, greater security, and better quality of education and health care at destinations influence the decision to migrate. Destinations inside and outside Africa therefore attract migrants with promises that origins cannot keep, and it is the interaction of push and pull factors that sets people in motion.

Migration in Africa's history and geography. Throughout its history Africa has experienced important migratory movements that contributed to its present-day demographic landscape, whether voluntarily or by force. The forced act of slave migration, compelled by European slave traders operating in Africa from the 16th to the 19th centuries, significantly reduced the total population of the continent. Moreover, in many parts of the continent, communities are found spread across two or three nation states, because the movement of people is often not limited by political boundaries.

keyTerms.def: The permanent change of residence by an individual or group of people, to establish a permanent or semi-permanent residence at a destination.
Movement within a country, for example from rural areas to the cities.
Movement of people from one country to another across an international boundary.
Migration undertaken by free choice, usually in search of better economic opportunities or the good life.
Migration of people expelled by factors such as war, drought, famine, natural disasters or political conflict.
A condition at the origin, such as poverty, low wages, unemployment, conflict or poor governance, that drives people to move away.
A condition at the destination, such as high income, security, or better education and health care, that attracts migrants.
The place to which migrants move to establish their new residence.

workedExamples.problem: Sort these conditions into push factors and pull factors: poverty, better quality of education, civil strife, high income at the destination, drought, greater security.
workedExamples.given: Six conditions; two categories: conditions at the origin versus conditions at the destination.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: push factors exist at the origin and drive people out; pull factors exist at the destination and beckon people in.
workedExamples.substitution: Poverty, civil strife and drought are hardships found at places people leave; education quality, income and security are advantages found at places people choose.
workedExamples.calculation: Matching each condition to its location of origin or destination sorts the list completely.
workedExamples.answer: Push: poverty, civil strife, drought. Pull: better quality of education, high income, greater security.

workedExamples.problem: A farm family leaves a drought-stricken lowland district and settles without plans to return. Identify the origin, the destination and the form of migration.
workedExamples.given: The family moves out of a rural district hit by drought and establishes a new, lasting residence elsewhere.
workedExamples.formula: Origin = the place left behind; destination = the new residence; form = voluntary or forced depending on the reason.
workedExamples.substitution: The lowland district is the origin; the place of settlement is the destination; drought is one of the factors that force people to move.
workedExamples.calculation: Because drought is a listed cause of forced migration, the movement cannot be classified as voluntary.
workedExamples.answer: Origin: the drought-stricken lowland; destination: the new settlement area; form: forced migration.

workedExamples.problem: A nurse accepts higher wages in another country, while a neighbouring family flees across the same border during civil conflict. Classify each movement.
workedExamples.given: One mover chooses better pay; the other is expelled by civil strife.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: voluntary migration seeks better opportunities; forced migration follows expulsion by human or natural pressures.
workedExamples.substitution: Wage-seeking is a free choice made for economic benefit; fleeing conflict matches the listed causes of forced migration.
workedExamples.calculation: Testing each case against the definitions fixes the correct label for both movers.
workedExamples.answer: The nurse's move is voluntary (international) migration; the family's flight is forced migration driven by civil strife.

commonMistakes: Listing conflicts and political instability as pull factors; these are push factors found at the origin.
Treating only movement across international borders as migration while forgetting internal rural-to-city moves.
Assuming all migration is voluntary when war, drought, famine and disasters clearly force people to move.
Believing political boundaries limit how African communities spread, when communities exist across two or three nation states.
Confusing the origin with the destination when identifying push and pull factors.
Thinking of migration as a single simple cause, when a complex web of push and pull factors underlies the process.
Forgetting that slave migration reduced Africa's total population, not that it only redistributed people.
applications: Interviewing a family that moved from a rural kebele to Addis Ababa and classifying their reasons as push or pull factors.
Mapping which Ethiopian towns attract internal migrants and evaluating whether jobs, security or services pull them.
Explaining how borderland communities in Africa live across two or three countries despite political boundaries.
Debating whether families displaced by drought in Ethiopia's lowlands are voluntary or forced migrants.
Linking rapid population growth in an origin district to unemployment and eventual out-migration.
Comparing the experiences of skilled and unskilled African workers who migrate because of poor governance and civil strife.
g10-geography-ug7-t2.summary: Migration is the permanent change of residence of individuals or groups and takes the forms of internal or international, voluntary or forced movement. Economic push factors such as poverty, low wages and unemployment, rooted in the mismatch between population growth and resources, combine with political pushes like conflict, corruption and instability, while destinations pull with higher income, security and better services. Africa's migratory history, including slave trade migrations from the 16th to 19th centuries, shrank the continent's population and left communities spread across nation states.

questions.explanation: They are political and social factors at the origin that push both skilled and unskilled workers to migrate.

questions.answer: rapid population growth outpaces available resources|population growth exceeds jobs and resources

Push factors worsen conditions at the origin

questions.explanation: The two distance categories are internal and international migration.

g10-geography-ug7-t3.overview: Africa's coasts and marine protected areas are under a high degree of threat as population growth, urbanization and industry concentrate along its shores. This lesson identifies the land-based and sea-based causes of coastal pollution, describes the major pollutant classes, and draws solutions from the plastic pollution case study.
objectives: Identify the land-based and sea-based sources of coastal pollution in Africa
Describe the major classes of pollutants reaching coastal waters
Explain why the sea's self-purification is limited and where pathogens survive
Analyze the effects of coastal pollution on habitats, people and the marine environment
Suggest solutions to coastal pollution using the plastic pollution case study
g10-geography-ug7-t3.simple: Coastal pollution enters the sea from human activities found both along coastlines and far inland. The most frequent cause is the discharge of municipal sewage and industrial waste into coastal waters and estuaries through low quality disposal facilities. Other sources include wastes dumped at sea, rubbish and sewage from ships, cargo handling, seabed exploitation and oil spills. The chief pollutant classes are decomposable organic materials, heavy metals and other toxic matter, inorganic substances, and pathogenic organisms. Rising population growth, urbanization and industrial development along African coasts make the threat worse. Plastic pollution illustrates the problem: Africa produces only 5 percent of the world's plastic but South Africa alone ranked 11th among ocean plastic polluters in 2010.
g10-geography-ug7-t3.detailed:
Sources of coastal pollution. Pollutants make their way into the ocean from human activities along coastlines and far inland. Pollution of coastal waters may arise from the discharge of sewage and industrial waste from coastal channels, dumping of wastes at sea, discharge of sewage and rubbish from ships, handling of cargo, exploration and exploitation of the sea bed and ocean floor, accidental pollution by oil spills, and pollutants carried from the land by air and other routes. Undoubtedly the most frequent cause is the discharge of municipal sewage and industrial wastes into coastal waters or into estuaries through low quality disposal facilities. If wastes contain persistent pollutants, discharge into rivers even at considerable distances upstream from the mouth can still send substantial quantities to the sea.

Pollutant classes and the sea's self-purification. The major classes of pollutant reaching coastal waters are decomposable organic materials, heavy metals and other toxic matter, dissolved and suspended non-toxic inorganic substances, and pathogenic organisms. Many factors, including dilution, temperature, adsorption, sedimentation and nutrient deficiencies, negatively affect the self-purification of the sea. The marine environment is generally unfavorable to the survival of most pathogenic organisms, yet under special circumstances, particularly in temperate and warm coastal waters near large cities, pathogenic agents can be found in the waters close to the coastline and in estuaries.

Why the problem is rising in Africa. The many people living in coastal zones, and even those far inland, generate large quantities of waste and other polluting substances that enter the seas directly or through coastal watersheds, rivers and precipitation from polluted air. Coastal pollution is rising rapidly as a result of population growth, urbanization and industrial development along many coastal areas of Africa, and the continent's coastlines and marine protected areas are under a high degree of threat from industrial wastes.

Effects on habitats and waters. The coastal marine environment is being affected by the modification and destruction of habitats, over-fishing and pollution, with many impacts traced back to land-based human activities located far from the sea. Many coastal waters carry excessive sediment and are contaminated by microbes and organic nutrients. Nitrogen, resulting from sewage discharges, agricultural and urban run-off and atmospheric precipitation, is a common problem, and the destruction of wetlands and mangroves, which act as natural filters for sediment, excessive nitrogen and wastes, has accelerated nutrient buildup. Further sources are oil leaks and accidental spills from shipping, discharge of bilgewater, oil drilling and mineral extraction, and some persistent pollutants are even reaching deep ocean waters.

The plastic case study. Plastic pollution is one of the greatest threats to life in oceans and seas worldwide, contributing to impacts on human health, loss of livelihoods, greenhouse gas emission, loss of biodiversity and compromised ecosystem functioning across Africa's land and seascapes. UNEP estimates put total global plastic production in 2020 at over 400 million tons, produced mostly in China (28 percent), North America (19 percent) and Western Europe (19 percent), which also lead consumption with 20, 21 and 18 percent respectively. Africa, with 1.3 billion people in 2020 (16 percent of the world population), produces 5 percent and consumes 4 percent of global plastic volumes, and its 2015 consumption was 16 kg per person against a global average of 45 kg and 136 kg in Western Europe. Yet in 2010 South Africa ranked 11th among the worst offenders for ocean plastic pollution, and according to WWF over 80 percent of South Africa's marine pollution originates from land-based sources: only 16 percent of its plastic is recycled, and roughly 8 million metric tons of discarded plastic reach rivers through wind, littering, improper waste management and overflowing landfills, and finally the ocean.

Toward solutions. The complexities of plastic pollution in coastal areas and estuaries require multi-stakeholder interventions and coordinated actions. Managing waste so that plastics and persistent pollutants never enter rivers, protecting wetlands and mangroves that naturally filter sediment and nitrogen, and involving governments, businesses, communities and researchers together are the practical directions that flow from this case study, since pollution that begins on land must be answered where land meets the sea.

keyTerms.def: The contamination of coastal waters and seas by wastes from coastal and inland human activities.
The release or flow of wastes, such as sewage and industrial effluent, into rivers, estuaries or coastal waters.
Wastewater and human waste from towns and cities, the most frequent single cause of coastal pollution problems.
Waste materials generated by factories and industry, discharged into coastal channels or dumped, threatening coastlines and marine protected areas.
Accidental releases of oil, from shipping and offshore activities, that pollute the marine environment.
The saltwater world of seas and oceans with the life and habitats it supports, which self-purifies only under limited conditions.
The land zone adjoining the sea where population growth, urbanization and industry concentrate and intensify pollution.
Disease-causing organisms, one of the four major pollutant classes, that survive in warm coastal waters near large cities and in estuaries.

workedExamples.problem: Using UNEP's 2020 estimate of over 400 million tons of plastics produced globally, calculate about how many tons Africa, which produces 5 percent of the global volume, generates.
workedExamples.given: Global plastic production in 2020 = 400 million tons; Africa's production share = 5% = 0.05.
workedExamples.formula: Africa's production = global production x Africa's share.
workedExamples.answer: About 20 million tons, a small share of global production yet enough to endanger Africa's own coastlines.

workedExamples.problem: Plastic consumption in Africa was 16 kg per person in 2015 against a global average of 45 kg per person. By how many kilograms does the African figure fall short, and roughly what fraction of the global average is it?
workedExamples.given: African consumption = 16 kg per person; global average = 45 kg per person.
workedExamples.formula: Difference = global average - African consumption; fraction = African consumption / global average.
workedExamples.answer: 29 kg less per person, about one-third of the global average, while Western Europe consumed 136 kg per person.

workedExamples.problem: A factory discharges persistent pollutants into a river 500 km upstream from the coast. Trace the pathway by which the sea becomes polluted.
workedExamples.given: The waste contains persistent pollutants; the river flows to a mouth that opens into the sea.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: wastes with persistent pollutants discharged into rivers, even far upstream, reach the sea in substantial quantities.
workedExamples.substitution: Pathway: factory discharge to river water to coastal watershed to estuary to coastal waters.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the pollutants persist, they are not broken down before the current carries them to and through the estuary.
workedExamples.answer: Pollutants travel far downstream, past the river mouth and estuary, into coastal waters, where they degrade fisheries and public health.

commonMistakes: Believing coastal pollution comes only from ships and beaches, when most pollutants originate on land, even far inland.
Forgetting that persistent pollutants poured into rivers far from the sea still travel downstream and pollute coastal waters.
Naming plastics as one of the four major pollutant classes in coastal waters; the listed classes are organic materials, heavy metals and toxic matter, inorganic substances and pathogens.
Assuming the sea purifies itself completely, when dilution, temperature, adsorption, sedimentation and nutrient deficiencies limit this process.
Ignoring the role of wetlands and mangroves, whose destruction as natural filters accelerates nutrient buildup.
Thinking Africa's low plastic consumption means it plays no ocean-pollution role; South Africa ranked 11th among worst offenders in 2010.
Believing more waste disposal pipes at the coast would fix everything, when low quality disposal facilities are themselves the leading cause.
applications: Identifying which Ethiopian towns upstream could pollute the seas through rivers that drain toward neighbouring coasts.
Urging protection of wetlands and mangroves as natural filters for sediment, nitrogen and wastes before they reach estuaries.
Advising a school or kebele on managing plastic waste properly so that wind and littering never carry it into rivers.
Relating nitrogen run-off from farms and towns near lakes to nutrient buildup and degraded waters.
Debating how the four pollutant classes affect fishing livelihoods along African coasts.
Using region-specific data, such as South Africa's 16 percent recycling rate, to argue for better waste systems in African cities.
g10-geography-ug7-t3.summary: Coastal pollution arises from land and sea sources, most frequently the discharge of municipal sewage and industrial wastes through low quality disposal facilities into coastal waters and estuaries, and its four major pollutant classes are organic materials, heavy metals and other toxic matter, inorganic substances and pathogens. Rapid population growth, urbanization and industrial development along African coasts are raising the threat to coastlines and marine protected areas, while destroyed wetlands and mangroves remove natural filters. The plastic case study shows that even low consuming regions can be major polluters, so coordinated multi-stakeholder action is needed.

questions.q: The most frequent cause of coastal pollution problems is:
options: discharge of municipal sewage and industrial wastes into coastal waters or estuaries
questions.explanation: The discharge of municipal sewage and industrial wastes through low quality disposal facilities is the most frequent cause.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT among the major classes of pollutants reaching coastal waters?
options: Heavy metals and other toxic matter
questions.explanation: The four classes are organic materials, heavy metals and toxic matter, inorganic substances, and pathogenic organisms.

questions.q: Persistent pollutants discharged into rivers far upstream from a river mouth can still reach the sea in substantial quantities.
questions.explanation: The textbook states that persistent pollutants discharged into rivers even far upstream reach the sea in substantial quantities.

questions.q: Which factor negatively affects the self-purification of the sea?
questions.explanation: Dilution, temperature, adsorption, sedimentation and nutrient deficiencies all negatively affect self-purification.

questions.q: Name the two natural coastal ecosystems whose destruction has accelerated nutrient buildup because they act as filters for sediment and wastes.
questions.explanation: Wetlands and mangroves act as natural filters for sediment, excessive nitrogen and wastes.

questions.q: Explain why coastal pollution can be traced to land-based human activities located far from the sea.
questions.answer: rivers and watersheds carry wastes to the sea|polluted air precipitates pollutants into seas
questions.explanation: Wastes generated inland enter seas through watersheds, rivers and precipitation from polluted air.

questions.q: According to the WWF, over 80 percent of marine pollution in South Africa originates from:
questions.explanation: Over 80 percent of South Africa's marine pollution comes from land-based sources.

questions.q: Africa produces about 5 percent and consumes about 4 percent of global plastic volumes.
questions.explanation: With 1.3 billion people in 2020, Africa produced 5 percent and consumed 4 percent of global plastic volumes.

questions.q: How much plastic, per person, was consumed in Africa in 2015?
questions.explanation: African plastic consumption in 2015 was 16 kg per person against a global average of 45 kg.

questions.q: Suggest two actions that could reduce coastal pollution in Africa, according to the case study and lesson.
questions.answer: better waste management and recycling|protect wetlands and mangroves|multi-stakeholder coordinated action
questions.explanation: Improved waste management and recycling, protecting wetlands and mangroves, and coordinated multi-stakeholder action all answer the problem.

questions.q: Why are pathogenic organisms a special risk in coastal waters near large cities?
options: They multiply fastest in cold polar seas
In temperate and warm coastal waters near large cities they survive near the coastline and in estuaries
They arrive only from cruise ships
They are killed instantly by salt water everywhere
questions.explanation: Although the marine environment is generally unfavorable to pathogens, in temperate and warm coastal waters near large cities they persist near the coastline and in estuaries.
